newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Fancied successor says backs Austrian chancellor.
newsitem.headline: Fancied successor says backs Austrian chancellor.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's heir apparent offered his support to the beleaguered Social Democrat Party leader on Friday but stopped short of saying he had no ambitions for the job.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima said he hoped Vranitzky, whose party scored its worst defeat since 1918 in European parliamentary elections last Sunday, would guide Austria through the EU presidency in 1998 and into an integrated Europe by the end of the century.
"It would be good if we could achieve our difficult goals, that is to say full employment and European economic integration, under Vranitzky's leadership," he told reporters.
But the former industrialist neatly sidestepped questions about his personal goals.
"I offered my services to the chancellor for two legislatory periods," was all Klima, 49, would say.
The reformed chain-smoker moved to the finance ministry from transport and state industry shortly after last December's general election.
Vranitzky, 59 and Europe's longest-serving government leader after Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany, has so far maintained a dignified silence amid growing calls for his resignation.

His party scored just 29.1 percent of the European parliamentary vote, falling behind coalition partner the People's Party for the first time in 30 years and finishing just 60,000 votes ahead of the far-right Freedom Party of Joerg Haider.
Since that dismal result some senior Social Democrats and normally supportive union bosses have called for a change in the party leadership after 10 years of continuity.

"The European electon result was a catastrophe. It is not enough to undertake a reform of party policy, heads must roll at the very top," said Hannes Androsch, a former Social Democrat finance minister and vice chancellor.
Austrian media and some of the party faithful have already begun touting Klima as Vranitzky's successor.
"I can certainly imagine Klima as chancellor," said former Vienna deputy mayor Hans Mayr, a Social Democrat.

During his three years at the ministry for transport and state industry Klima oversaw the sale of state-owned industry, winning around some of privatisation's fiercest critics with a combination of toughness and charm.
Voter surveys show he has a high profile with the electorate and ranks among Austria's most popular politicians.
Austrian media have forecast Vranitzky will step down within the next 12 months. Other favourites to take over at the chancellery are Vienna mayor Michael Hauepl and Androsch.
